newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraqi envoy says UN food deliveries much too late.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi envoy says UN food deliveries much too late.

text.p: Iraq's U.N. ambassador, Nizar Hamdoon, on Monday complained to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan that deliveries of humanitarian goods, particularly food, had been held up by U.N. bodies much too long.

Iraq, he said, had not received a single bit of food or other goods under the so-called oil-for-food plan that went into affect on December 10. But he told reporters after seeing Annan that there had been no difficulties from the U.N. Security Council's sanctions committee in approving oil contracts.
He said certain contracts for goods had been suspended "without letting us know why so that we could clarify it."
He said he also wanted to make sure that the money allocated for the suspended contracts would not be used to pay other vendors as he suspected was currently the case.
"We are today more than two months from...the start (of the deal) and no kilo of rice or sugar or whatever has really arrived in Iraq," he said.
"They are expecting something to arrive in March. I only reflected on the frustration that we are having in Iraq on this operation," he added.

Under the "oil-for-food" agreement between Iraq and the United Nations, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian items to mitigate the effects of strict sanctions in force since Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Hamdoon said most of the delays were "technical" in nature but that did not alleviate Iraq's frustration in not receiving the goods. He said Annan promised "to do whatever is needed to speed things up."

The contracts are approved by the council's sanctions committee while the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs is sending inspectors to monitor whether the food is distributed equitably. The inspectors began to arrive in Iraq last week.
Asked which U.N. department was responsible, Hamdoon said, "I am not here to try to spread out accusations but the whole process is very cumbersome."
He said he did not mention any problems with Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, whose final accounting is delaying any eventual lifting of the oil embargo entirely.
